title: From flat faces to a round form
say: Welcome back! The cube helped us notice flat faces. Now we’ll explore a sphere, where light changes gently across a curved surface. We’ll build the circle, find the shadow, and bring out that roundness. This is one useful drawing skill, not a test of whether you’re an artist. Take it a little at a time. I’m here with you.
hint: The Sphere · Your paper, your pace

title: Meet six zones of light
say: Look for the highlight, the brightest spot. Halftones carry us across the lit side. The terminator is where direct light ends; just inside the shadow, we find the darker core shadow. Reflected light gently lifts part of the shadow, but stays darker than the lit side. The cast shadow falls onto the table. Tap a label to find it. We’ll meet these again as we draw.
hint: Tap a zone to find it

title: Let the light move
say: Move the light from side to side. Notice how the bright area moves and the cast shadow stretches away from it. Unlike the cube, this form has no sharp corner between its light and dark sides. Try the slider. There is no wrong answer here.
hint: Move the sun

title: Your pencils and paper
say: Keep your pencils, sketch paper, erasers, and a blending stump or tissue nearby. Harder pencils help with light construction. HB and softer pencils let us build tone gradually. Leave your paper’s brightest area clean. If you need the full setup again, Preparation is there for you.
hint: Light construction · Gentle layers

title: Settle in and begin
say: Let your shoulders relax. You don’t need a perfect circle on the first try. Watch the teacher, then make one small change on your own page. I’ll stop at the important moments and wait for you to press Continue.
hint: Watch · Try · Continue

title: Define the sphere placement
say: Let’s pause here. Start by ghosting four light marks where the sphere will sit. These four marks define the size and position. Leave breathing room around the edges of your paper.
hint: Mark top, bottom, left, right — plus paper margin.

title: Measure left and right
say: Let’s pause here. Hold your pencil horizontally. Measure from the center to the left mark, then to the right mark. They should be equal — if not, adjust.
hint: Use your pencil to compare distances from the center.

title: Measure top and bottom
say: Let’s pause here. Rotate your pencil vertically. Compare distance from center to top, then to bottom. Equal distances = a true sphere, not an oval.
hint: Now check vertically — same pencil method.

title: Find the diagonal points
say: Let’s pause here. Use the same pencil-radius to locate four diagonal guide points (NE, NW, SE, SW). These eight points together define the circle.
hint: Same radius — now on the diagonals.

title: See the full framework
say: Let’s pause here. This is the scaffolding underneath every well-drawn sphere. The cross gives you center. The eight points give you the curve. Trust the structure.
hint: Center cross + diameter + radius + 8 guide points.

title: Cut with straight tangents first
say: Let’s pause here. Beginner mistake: drawing a curve straight away. Instead, connect your eight points with short straight lines first. A circle is just many small straight cuts.
hint: Connect points with short straight lines — not curves yet.

title: Refine into a clean curve
say: Let’s pause here. Once your tangent cuts are right, gently round the corners. Don't force perfection — let the curve emerge from the geometry you built.
hint: Now soften the straight cuts into a smooth circle.

title: Your circle framework
say: Check this part of your drawing beside the teacher’s example. Make any small adjustments you want. There is no timer. Continue when you are ready.
hint: Your turn · Take your time

title: Your circle framework
say: You’ve taken a blank page and given your sphere a place to live. That careful measuring matters. Take a breath, loosen your hand, and let’s find the light.
hint: One thoughtful step forward ✓

title: Erase the cutting lines
say: Let’s pause here. After cutting the sphere with straight tangents, use your eraser to clean away the leftover construction lines. This refinement makes the outer edge feel round, smooth, and natural — not geometric.
hint: Clean up the outer edge — make the circle round and natural.

title: Cast shadow + sphere together
say: Let’s pause here. Draw the cast shadow at the same time as you finish the sphere. They're not two separate elements — they're one connected structure. The shadow grounds the sphere; the sphere casts the shadow.
hint: The shadow is part of the same system as the sphere.

title: Mark the terminator line
say: Let’s pause here. As soon as the form is drawn, use the terminator line to clearly separate the light side from the shadow side. This single line is what makes a sphere read as three-dimensional.
hint: Divide the sphere — light side vs shadow side.

title: Strengthen the terminator
say: Let’s pause here. Return to the terminator line and reinforce it. Strengthening this boundary is what creates strong contrast between the light side and the shadow side — and that contrast is what gives the sphere its volume.
hint: Go back to the terminator and darken it more.

title: Sharpen the shadow contrast
say: Let’s pause here. Now move to the cast shadow below the sphere and strengthen its main contrast line. Making the shadow side firmly darker than the light side is what completes the illusion of form sitting in space.
hint: Push the cast shadow darker — make the contrast clear.

title: Light and shadow connected
say: Check this part of your drawing beside the teacher’s example. Make any small adjustments you want. There is no timer. Continue when you are ready.
hint: Your turn · Take your time

title: Light and shadow connected
say: You’ve connected the sphere to its shadow. It’s beginning to feel like something sitting on a table. Keep going at your own pace.
hint: One thoughtful step forward ✓

title: Tone inside the terminator
say: Let’s pause here. Begin laying tone strictly within the terminator. Don't let your pencil cross over into the light side. This boundary is what gives the sphere its volume.
hint: Stay inside the dark side — build tone within the terminator line.

title: Strengthen the terminator
say: Return to the core-shadow band just inside the light–shadow boundary. Deepen it gently, while keeping the transition soft. The contact shadow beneath the sphere may be darker still. Try this on your drawing, then continue when you are ready.
hint: Reinforce the terminator — keep it the darkest, most concentrated line.

title: Tone the shadow as one family
say: Let’s pause here. Tone the cast shadow alongside the sphere, not separately. Sphere and shadow belong to the same value family — they should be developed together so they feel unified, not pasted together.
hint: Fill the cast shadow at the same time — same value family as the sphere.

title: Anchor the sphere to the surface
say: Let’s pause here. Once the cast shadow is filled, return to the area where the sphere meets the surface and push that contrast hard. This is the darkest part of the cast shadow — it's what makes the sphere feel grounded, not floating.
hint: Strengthen the contact area — make the sphere sit on the table.

title: Shadow gradation — near to far
say: Let’s pause here. Finish by strengthening the shadow nearest to us, then gradate it lighter as it moves away. This near-to-far gradation stretches the perception of space — the shadow becomes the tool that pulls the eye into depth.
hint: Closest part of the shadow = darkest. Gradate outward to extend depth.

title: A grounded sphere
say: Check this part of your drawing beside the teacher’s example. Make any small adjustments you want. There is no timer. Continue when you are ready.
hint: Your turn · Take your time

title: A grounded sphere
say: You’ve built a shadow family with gentle layers. Look back at the light area you protected. That contrast is doing useful work.
hint: One thoughtful step forward ✓

title: Build the light-gray halftone band
say: Let’s pause here. This is the halftone area — a band of value that extends from the terminator into the light side. Wrap it gently around the whole sphere. Switch to a lighter pencil (HB or 2H) — this is not a line, it's an entire surface that helps the light side transition naturally.
hint: Wrap a light gray band from terminator into the light side.

title: Cross-hatch to unify the tones
say: Let’s pause here. When you tone over your own strokes in the same direction, the result can feel rigid. Mrs. Dawn now adds strokes in the opposite direction — cross-hatching. This blending pass unifies the earlier tones into a softer, more continuous surface.
hint: Hatch against your previous stroke direction to blend values.

title: Soften the terminator into the shadow
say: Let’s pause here. A common mistake: drawing the terminator as a sharp, rigid line or block. Mrs. Dawn pushes that area repeatedly — not just darkening it, but also blending it gradually into the shadow side. The terminator should feel like a natural transition, not a wall.
hint: Don't leave the terminator as a hard line — connect it to the dark side.

title: It's a terminator BAND, not a line
say: Let’s pause here. Look carefully — Mrs. Dawn defines a clear terminator AREA, not a terminator line. This band acts as a bridge between the light side and the shadow side. It's what makes the sphere pop forward in 3D, and it's the key visual link between the two value zones.
hint: The dark-light boundary is a surface, not an edge.

title: Switch to 2B for stronger work
say: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn explicitly switches to a 2B pencil. The HB has carried you this far; the 2B will let you push the values that need to feel firmer and richer.
hint: Change pencils — now 2B for the deeper details.

title: Radiate from the terminator outward
say: Let’s pause here. With 2B, Mrs. Dawn strengthens transitions in both directions — from the terminator toward the light side, and from the terminator toward the dark side. This radiating gradient is what gives the sphere strong perspective. She also strengthens the cast shadow with the same pencil.
hint: Use 2B to spread values from the terminator into both light and dark.

title: Bring out the blender
say: Let’s pause here. Mrs. Dawn introduces a blending tool — a blending stump if you have one, or a tissue or napkin works fine. This tool unifies and softens all the tones you've built up. The drawing should feel more like a smooth surface than a series of pencil strokes.
hint: Blender / tissue / napkin — softens the whole surface.

title: Follow your stroke direction
say: Let’s pause here. Important: when blending, follow the direction of your pencil strokes. Sweep gently in the same direction. Do not press hard, and do not blend randomly across the surface — that creates a muddy, dirty drawing. Light, directional sweeps only.
hint: Blend along the direction of your strokes — never randomly.

title: Optional: re-touch with HB
say: Let’s pause here. This step is optional but recommended. Mrs. Dawn returns to the HB pencil and gently presses the strongest tones back into the paper. This subtly tightens the whole drawing and makes it feel more natural — less like raw pencil, more like a unified surface.
hint: Press strong tones back into the paper with light HB strokes.

title: A softly rounded form
say: You’ve worked through structure, shadow, and soft transitions. Take a moment to notice one change you’re pleased with. Your effort deserves that pause.
hint: One thoughtful step forward ✓

title: Take this with you
say: Look at an apple, a face under a lamp, or the moon. Can you notice light turning into shadow? That’s something you’ve practised today. And here’s a thought to keep: does making a drawing accurate automatically make it beautiful? You don’t need to answer now. Keep looking, and stay curious.
hint: What do you notice now?

title: You stayed with your drawing
say: You’ve explored the sphere, one step at a time. Your drawing doesn’t need to be perfect to be worth celebrating. Press Continue and Artchi has a little reward for you. Then you can carry your new observations into the cylinder.
hint: The Sphere · Ready to celebrate
